Constantine the Great. A Roman emperor who ruled from AD 306 to 337. He emerged victorious from the civil wars following the collapse of the Tetrarchy to become the sole ruler of the Roman Empire. His reign was a major turning point in history, as he became the first Roman emperor to convert to Christianity and moved the imperial capital to a newly founded city in the East.

Before the Battle of the Milvian Bridge against Maxentius, he supposedly saw a cross in the sky with the words "in this sign, you will conquer." Together with Licinius, he issued the Edict of Milan in AD 313, which granted religious tolerance to Christianity and ended official state persecution. He convened the First Council of Nicaea in AD 325 to address the Arian controversy, which resulted in the Nicene Creed, affirming that the Son is of the same substance as the Father. He founded a new imperial capital on the site of ancient Byzantium, naming it Constantinople, which is modern-day Istanbul, and this shift the empire's centre of gravity eastward. Though he converted to Christianity, he delayed his official baptism until he was on his deathbed.

His predecessor Diocletian established the Tetrarchic system that Constantine eventually dismantled. Licinius was his co-emperor in the East whom he eventually defeated in civil war to become sole ruler. Julian the Apostate, his nephew and a future emperor, would briefly attempt to return the empire to paganism.
